description: This case study summarises a Yale School of the Environment study of tap water quality in Jackson, Mississippi, after the 2022 failure of the city water system left more than 150,000 residents without reliable safe drinking water and under boil water notices for months. Researchers collected tap water samples from homes and businesses, focusing on locations with young children, older adults or other vulnerable people, using the EPA updated Lead and Copper Rule protocol, and tested metals, disinfectant chemistry and corrosion indicators. All samples met federal primary standards for lead and copper, yet every site exceeded secondary standards, seven sites had chloride-to-sulfate ratios signalling corrosion potential, and first-draw samples carried the highest lead. The authors conclude that system-level compliance can hide localised risk, which clusters in homes with older plumbing. The paper appears in the journal Water; this record describes the university news article, which is the page read. Coverage: the Jackson metropolitan area after 2022, a sample, not a census. Access: free web page; licence not stated. Caveats: the sample is small and targeted, and the news article does not give the sample size or the paper's data access terms. It supports drinking water vulnerability, equity and corrosion-risk analysis after a system failure, and relates to the EPA SDWIS compliance records in the catalogue.
